summary: Specifies a transition mechanism that translates between IPv4 and IPv6 packet headers and ICMP messages without keeping per-connection state. It is a standards-track document at the proposed standard level, and it was replaced by RFC 6145.

plainLanguage.summary: It is a translator that swaps old and new address formats on each message and does not need to remember the conversation.

questions: how to translate ipv4 to ipv6 headers
how does stateless ip translation work
why are ipv4 options not translated
subtitle: Translate between IPv4 and IPv6 packets without keeping per-connection state.

tldr.problem: As IPv4 addresses run out, IPv6-only devices need to communicate with IPv4-only devices. A translator would need to remember state for every connection, adding complexity and scaling limits.
tldr.mechanism: SIIT translates IPv4 and IPv6 packet headers independently, one packet at a time, without storing any state. Each packet carries the information needed to be translated correctly. IPv4 addresses are mapped to special IPv6 addresses and vice versa.
tldr.outcome: SIIT enabled IPv6-only networks to coexist with IPv4-only networks during early IPv6 transition. RFC 2765 was replaced by RFC 6145 with refinements. Stateless translation remains useful for specific scenarios but has been partially superseded by stateful techniques like DNS64 and NAT64.

today: RFC 2765 is obsoleted by RFC 6145, which clarifies and refines the stateless translation algorithm. While SIIT enabled early IPv6 transition scenarios, modern deployments often use stateful techniques like NAT64 combined with DNS64 for IPv4/IPv6 interoperability. Stateless translation remains valuable for specific use cases, particularly in enterprise and research networks.

sections.title: The Transition Problem
sections.content:
The Internet is transitioning from IPv4 (32-bit addresses) to IPv6 (128-bit addresses). Early in this transition, some networks have IPv6-only devices while parts of the Internet still speak only IPv4. These two worlds need to communicate. Simply assigning every device both an IPv4 and IPv6 address is wasteful because IPv4 addresses are scarce.

The challenge is bridging IPv6-only devices to IPv4-only devices without stateful intermediaries. A stateful translator would need to track each connection, which creates a single point of failure, prevents redundancy, and does not scale well. SIIT solves this by making translation completely stateless: each translator processes each packet independently, translating headers and addresses based on the packet contents alone.
sections.plainLanguage: Some new devices speak only IPv6, but many old devices speak only IPv4. SIIT lets them talk without the translator having to remember anything about their conversation.

sections.title: How SIIT Works: Addresses and Mapping
sections.content:
SIIT introduces a new form of IPv6 address: the IPv4-translated address (format 0::ffff:0:a.b.c.d). This differs from the IPv4-mapped address (::ffff:a.b.c.d), which refers to IPv4-only nodes. When an IPv6-only host needs to reach an IPv4 node, it uses an IPv4-mapped address as the destination. When an IPv4 node sends packets back, they are translated to have an IPv4-translated address as the destination so they reach the right IPv6 node.

The translator operates at the edge of networks, converting IPv4 packets to IPv6 and vice versa. It must know which pool of IPv4 addresses represent IPv6-only nodes so it knows when translation is needed. The IPv6 network inside assumes IPv6-to-IPv6 connectivity (which may use tunnels); routing gets the packets to the translator, which converts them at the boundary.
sections.plainLanguage: IPv4-translated addresses are special IPv6 addresses that represent IPv6 devices on the IPv4 side of the translator. The translator looks at the address and knows when to convert between the two formats.

sections.title: Translating from IPv4 to IPv6
sections.content:
When the translator receives an IPv4 packet destined for a device in the IPv4-translated address pool, it converts the IPv4 header to an IPv6 header. The IPv4 source address becomes the lower 32 bits of an IPv4-mapped IPv6 address (::ffff:source). The IPv4 destination address becomes the lower 32 bits of an IPv4-translated IPv6 address (0::ffff:0:destination). The IPv4 TTL becomes the IPv6 Hop Limit.

IPv6 requires path MTU discovery (routers never fragment; only the sender can). If the IPv4 packet has the DF (Do Not Fragment) bit set, no fragment header is added. If DF is not set and the resulting IPv6 packet would exceed 1280 bytes, the translator fragments it so the IPv6 packet fits in 1280 bytes (which is guaranteed never to need fragmentation). For ICMP packets, the translator must also recompute the checksum and translate ICMP error messages, including the embedded IP headers.
sections.plainLanguage: To convert IPv4 to IPv6: take the source and destination addresses, wrap them in special IPv6 formats, and change the header fields. Handle fragmentation carefully because IPv6 has stricter rules.

sections.title: Translating from IPv6 to IPv4
sections.content:
When the translator receives an IPv6 packet from an IPv6-only node destined for an IPv4 node, it reverses the process. The IPv4-translated source address (0::ffff:0:a.b.c.d) is converted back to an IPv4 address (a.b.c.d). The IPv4-mapped destination address (::ffff:a.b.c.d) is converted to IPv4 form. The IPv6 Hop Limit becomes the IPv4 TTL. The IPv6 traffic class can be copied to the IPv4 ToS field.

If an IPv6 fragment header is present, the translator must extract the fragment offset and reassembly id. If the IPv6 source address is not in the IPv4-translated pool, the packet is invalid and should be discarded. Like IPv4-to-IPv6 translation, ICMPv6 messages require special handling: the translator must translate the ICMP type and code values, recompute checksums, and translate embedded IPv6 headers.
sections.plainLanguage: Converting IPv6 back to IPv4 unwraps the addresses and converts the header fields back. ICMPv6 error messages need special care because the packet inside them also needs translating.

sections.title: What SIIT Cannot Do
sections.content:
SIIT has several important limitations. It does not translate IPv4 options or IPv6 extension headers like routing headers and hop-by-hop options. Multicast is not supported because IPv4 multicast addresses cannot be cleanly mapped to IPv6 multicast addresses. Source routing cannot be translated correctly because IPv6 and IPv4 use different semantics.

IPsec's Authentication Header (AH) cannot work end-to-end through SIIT because AH covers the IPv4 identification field, which the translator cannot predict. However, ESP in transport mode can work because it does not cover the outer IP header, only the encrypted payload. Fragmented UDP packets with zero checksums are not translated because UDP requires a checksum in IPv6, and the translator cannot compute it for fragments without maintaining state.
sections.plainLanguage: SIIT handles basic packets well but cannot translate everything. Options, routing headers, multicast, and some security protocols do not work through a stateless translator.

left.title: IPv4-mapped
left.desc: Refers to IPv4-only nodes; used for destinations of packets to IPv4 devices.

right.title: IPv4-translated
right.desc: Refers to IPv6-only nodes; used for destinations of packets from IPv4 devices.
